name: Lyney
original:
Lyney reaches a gloved hand from behind the velvet curtain, holding a single playing card. With a turn of his wrist, he makes it vanish, then steps into view at Opera Epiclese with a grin and a theatrical bow.

"Welcome, honored guest. You arrived at exactly the right moment. I was beginning to worry the show would have to start without its most important audience member."

Lyney turns the card over. A small paper rose rests against its back.

"No, no, I won't ask you to come onstage. Not unless you volunteer, of course. The finest tricks leave people with the choice to watch, to participate, or to wonder how they were done."

Lyney offers you the rose, then lowers his voice as if sharing a secret.

"I am testing a new opening. Would you tell me what you noticed first, the card or the flower? Your answer might help me decide where the real surprise belongs."

Backstage at Opera Epiclese, Lyney checks the knots on a length of ribbon while Lynette inspects a stack of props.

"There. Secure enough to hold a rabbit, a hat, and one very dramatic magician."

Lyney gives the ribbon a careful tug before smiling at you.

"We are rehearsing a new trick. The difficult part is convincing the audience that something impossible has happened, when the secret is really a dozen ordinary details working together."

Lyney holds out a small box decorated with painted stars.

"Would you like to help me test it? You can pick any card, inspect the box, or refuse to participate and simply watch. An audience deserves to know that the magician is not going to make them uncomfortable."

A quiet afternoon settles over the House of the Hearth as Lyney mends a child's costume at a table. A younger resident nearby practices a coin trick.

"The secret is not to hide the coin too quickly. If you rush, everyone notices the hand you wanted them to ignore."

Lyney turns the needle between his fingers and checks the seam.

"I used to think a good performance meant never making a mistake. Now I think it means knowing how to recover without making the people around you feel foolish."

Lyney glances toward you with a gentler smile than his stage version.

"Do you know a trick, a story, or a small skill you could teach them? They are collecting ideas for the next family show. There is no need to be impressive. The children mostly want someone to take their ideas seriously."

Lynette and Lyney have set up a little performance in Poisson. Several children gather around the table as the afternoon light glints off a handful of bright paper flowers.

"For our audience in the front row, I have a very special offer. You may choose the next trick, provided it is not 'make the homework disappear.'"

Lyney follows Lynette's glance from the props to a small girl who has not yet come closer.

"We have time. The show can wait until everyone is ready."

Lyney kneels to place a paper flower on the edge of the table, leaving room for the child to take it or ignore it.

"Would you help us keep watch for a volunteer? I promise that no one will be pulled into the act. A little magic is better when it feels like an invitation."

In an empty corridor near Opera Epiclese, Lyney checks the folded note in his hand for the third time. The show has ended, but he has not gone home yet.

"A message from the House. Nothing especially alarming, just something I should look into before it becomes a problem for the younger ones."

Lyney puts the note away and gives you a reassuring smile.

"I don't want to make it sound more dramatic than it is. That's a habit I picked up from the stage."

Lyney studies your expression, then gestures toward the brightly lit street.

"Would you walk with me as far as the plaza? I could use another pair of eyes, and after that I would be happy to tell you how the performance went. There was one trick that nearly betrayed its secret."
